# `liber:display@1`

Generated reference for the `liber:display` package (`display.lsidl`). See [the LSIDL language](../../../LSIDL.md).

LiberSystem display package - capability-scoped surfaces with their own present queues.  ONE CONNECTION, MANY SURFACES. The previous contract said "one display connection owns at most one surface" and put `acquire`, `present`, `release` and `input-focus` at connection level. Every desktop and mobile application is more than one surface - a main window, a dialog, a popup, a menu, a tooltip, a video surface, offscreen content - so that object model is one a compositor would have to break. A surface is its own capability here, with its own queue, its own events and its own configuration.  AND THERE IS NO COMPATIBILITY PATH. Nothing is versioned before the first release and no external software depends on this; a compatibility shim would be a second object model to keep correct.  EVERY ANSWER HERE IS `WSI Profile 1`'s. The twelve configuration fields, the six events, the four image states and eight transitions, the four acquire answers, the four present outcomes, the nine damage rules and the two completion pairs are frozen in `docs/graphics/WSI_PROFILE_1.md`; this package is how they are spelled on the wire.

## Types

### resource `image-object`

A PRESENTABLE IMAGE THE CLIENT CREATED, for the service to compose from.  THE SUPPLIER ALLOCATES AND THE SUPPLIER PAYS. `SYS_MEMORY_OBJECT_CREATE` charges the Domain that CREATED the object, and the charge stays with it when the capability moves - so a service that allocated its clients' images would pay for every one of them, and one client could exhaust the service's quota while its own budget still looked healthy. That is the accounting defect this contract exists to remove, and the answer is that the queue's images come from the client.  WHAT IS GUARANTEED IS THAT NO DOMAIN PAYS FOR STORAGE IT DID NOT ITSELF ALLOCATE, and not that the paying Domain is the requesting one: `ObjectInfo` carries koid, type, rights, generation and size and NO charged Domain, so the service cannot tell a client-created object from one a third Domain created and handed over. Sponsorship is therefore possible and is a capability-system consequence rather than a hole - it requires that Domain to allocate and transfer deliberately, which is what a capability IS.  `@kernel(memory-object)` is what makes the `@rights` guard on `provide-image` refuse a handle of any other kernel object rather than checking rights on whatever it was handed.

An opaque kernel object, transferred as `handle<image-object>`.

### record `scale-ratio`

THE SCALE IS A RATIO AND NEVER A FLOAT ON THE WIRE.  A fractional scale that two sides round differently produces an off-by-one extent, and that is the bug that shows as a one-pixel seam nobody can reproduce. With the ratio, both neighbours of a shared edge compute the same integer from the same two integers.

| `denominator` | `u32` |  |

### record `output-colour`

WHAT THE OUTPUT CAN ACTUALLY SHOW, which a colour-space NAME does not say.  A tone map sends one luminance to one, and WHICH luminance that is depends on the display: a two-thousand-nit highlight on a two-hundred-nit panel and on a thousand-nit one are two different curves. A conversion that does not know the destination's luminance is guessing at the one number that decides how the image looks.  EVERY LUMINANCE IS OPTIONAL AND `none` IS NOT ZERO. A display that does not report what it can do is the ordinary case - nothing here asks a panel yet, because DDC needs a bus no driver can reach - and `Image and Colour Profile 1` says absent HDR metadata is a refusal to assume rather than a default to invent.

### record `surface-configuration`

ONE ATOMIC SNAPSHOT OF EVERYTHING THAT DECIDES HOW A CLIENT DRAWS.  THE FIELDS TRAVEL TOGETHER OR THE CLIENT RENDERS AT A SIZE NOTHING ASKED FOR. A client that applied a new scale with an old extent would lay out for a window that does not exist, which is the whole reason this is a snapshot rather than a set of events.  THE PHYSICAL EXTENT IS THE AUTHORITATIVE ONE and the logical extent is derived from it and the scale, never the other way round - so a rounding difference cannot make the two disagree.

### record `display-resources`

WHAT THE DISPLAY PATH HOLDS THAT THE KERNEL CHARGES NOBODY FOR.  A PRESENTABLE IMAGE IS A MEMORYOBJECT and is charged to the Domain that created it, which under this contract is the client's. EVERYTHING ELSE here - the surface record, its queue slots, its pending-present list, its event stream and its place in the service's wait vector - is service heap and a service wait set, charged to nobody. Those are exactly what an adversarial client can multiply, so each is reported with the bound it is held to.  OBSERVATION AND NEVER ENFORCEMENT. Reading these changes nothing; the bounds are enforced where the structures are allocated, and a reader that found a count at its bound has learned that a client is being refused rather than caused it to be.  AND NEVER IMAGE CONTENTS. There is no field here from which a pixel can be recovered: what a surface SHOWS is not an observability question.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `surfaces` | `u64` | Live surfaces across every connection, and the service-wide ceiling. |
| `surface-bound` | `u64` |  |
| `present-images` | `u64` | Queue slots across every surface, supplied or not, and the most one surface may negotiate. |
| `image-bound` | `u64` |  |
| `queued-presents` | `u64` | Accepted presents not yet settled, and the most one surface may have outstanding. |
| `present-bound` | `u64` |  |
| `damage-entries` | `u64` | Damage rectangles this service RETAINS, and the most one present may carry.  THE LIVE COUNT IS ZERO IN THIS IMPLEMENTATION AND THAT IS THE POINT: damage lives for the duration of the present call that carried it and is never stored, so there is nothing here for a client to multiply. An implementation that deferred presents would retain them, and this is the field it would have to report. |
| `damage-bound` | `u64` |  |
| `waiters` | `u64` | Handles this service's one progress loop waits on, and the kernel's ceiling on a wait set. |
| `waiter-bound` | `u64` |  |
| `resets` | `u64` | How many times the display path has been RESET: a scanout adopted after the previous one went away. A machine whose GPU driver keeps restarting shows it here. |
| `faulted` | `bool` | Whether this service currently has NO scanout at all - the fault state, which is different from a reset that succeeded. |

## Interfaces

### interface `display-stats`

OBSERVATION AND NEVER ENFORCEMENT: what the display path holds, for the System Graph.  A SEPARATE INTERFACE AND NOT A `display-admin` OPERATION, because authority to READ what a service holds must not be authority to bind a process to a display or to take the screen. The System Graph is handed this endpoint and nothing else, which is what makes "never as enforcement" a property of the capability rather than a promise about the caller.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `resources` | `resources() -> display-resources` |  |

### interface `surface`

ONE SURFACE: its own queue, its own events, its own configuration.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `configuration` | `configuration() -> result<surface-configuration, error>` | The current configuration. A client that missed the event can ask. |
| 2 | `ack-configure` | `ack-configure(serial: u64) -> result<unit, error>` | Acknowledge a configuration by serial, which is what the lifecycle turns on: `configure -> rebuild -> ack -> first present Full`. A stale or unknown serial is refused. |
| 3 | `queue` | `queue() -> result<present-queue, error>` | The present queue for the current generation: how many images it has, their pitch, the generation they belong to and the two completion endpoints. Calling it again after a generation change is how a client rebuilds. |
| 4 | `acquire-next` | `acquire-next() -> result<acquired-image, error>` | Take the next image, WITHOUT BLOCKING. |
| 5 | `abandon` | `abandon(image: u32) -> result<unit, error>` | Give an acquired image back WITHOUT presenting it.  THE EDGE AN IMPLEMENTATION FORGETS. A client that acquired and then decided not to draw - a resize arrived, the window closed - must have a way back that is not a present, or a resized window leaks an image per resize. |
| 6 | `present` | `present(image: u32, serial: u64, generation: u64, damage: damage-region) -> result<u64, error>` | Submit an acquired image. IT CONSUMES THE IMAGE: there is no safe path back to the pixels.  THE PRESENT NAMES ITS CONFIGURATION SERIAL AND ITS IMAGE GENERATION, and both must match the acknowledged current configuration at acceptance - which is what stops a frame drawn for one size from being shown at another.  DAMAGE IS A HINT AND NEVER PERMISSION. Every presented image contains a COMPLETE VALID FRAME; the damage says which pixels changed against the previously presented one. An empty list means nothing changed and the present is still ordered and still completes. The whole surface is the `full` variant and never one rectangle covering the extent, because a rectangle can be wrong by a pixel and a variant cannot. A rectangle outside the extent is a typed refusal and never a silent clamp. |
| 7 | `events` | `events() -> stream<surface-event>` | The live event stream: configuration, image availability, per-present completion, close requests, visibility and focus. |
| 8 | `input-focus` | `input-focus() -> result<handle<channel>, error>` | The one-shot proof channel for this surface's input focus. The client transfers it to `input.subscribe-keys`; a surface without focus has no proof, and a focus change revokes the previous peer. |
| 9 | `close` | `close() -> result<unit, error>` | Drop the surface and everything it owns. |
| 10 | `provide-image` | `provide-image(index: u32, image: handle<image-object>) -> result<unit, error>` | SUPPLY one image of the current generation's queue: a MemoryObject the CLIENT created, of at least `pitch * height` bytes.  A V1 PRESENTABLE IMAGE IS COHERENT CPU-VISIBLE MEMORY: a send is a release and a receive is an acquire, in both directions, and there is no explicit flush in the contract because there is no non-coherent import in v1.  THE SERVICE NEEDS `read` AND `map` AND DOES NOT NEED `write`. It composes FROM these pixels and never into them, the client keeps its own handles, and the service never transfers an imported image onward - which is what makes delegation a decision rather than an accident.  A PARTIALLY SUPPLIED QUEUE IS A QUEUE THAT CANNOT BE PRESENTED FROM, so `acquire-next` answers `again` until every index has been provided. An index past the negotiated count, a slot already filled for this generation, or an object shorter than the layout needs is a typed refusal - and a generation change releases the whole set, because no image ever crosses a generation. |

### interface `display-admin`

Privileged launcher boundary. PermissionManager transfers the Process capability returned by ProcessService and receives a fresh display connection bound to that exact process. Ordinary display clients never receive this interface and cannot bind themselves or another task; emergency revocation signals the bound task.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `bind` | `bind(task: handle<task>) -> result<handle<channel>, error>` | The task handle must already carry `manage`, which is what a `task` capability IS: binding a display to a process it cannot manage would hand out a connection whose emergency revocation - signalling the bound task - could not be carried out.  AND `wait`, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME OWNERSHIP. Cleanup cannot be left to the connection's channel: a channel stays open while ANYONE holds its peer, so a surface's imported images would outlive the process the contract says owns them. A waitable task is how the service learns that process ended, independently of channel peer lifetime and of whether the display driver is making progress. |
| 2 | `stats` | `stats() -> presentation-stats` |  |
| 3 | `set-visible` | `set-visible(task: handle<task>, surface: u64) -> result<unit, error>` | Make one surface the visible, scanout-bound one. THE VISIBILITY RULE IS THE SERVICE'S AND NOT A CLIENT'S: a client that could make itself visible is a client that can take the screen. |
| 4 | `set-scale` | `set-scale(scale: scale-ratio) -> result<unit, error>` | THE OUTPUT'S SCALE, AND IT IS THE SYSTEM'S TO CHOOSE.  A client lays out in LOGICAL pixels and rasterises PHYSICAL ones, and the ratio between them is a property of the output and the person looking at it - not of the application. A client that could set it would be a client that decides how much memory every other client's images need, so it is here beside `set-visible` for the same reason that one is: both are answers only something holding the whole screen may give.  WHAT CHANGES AND WHAT DOES NOT. Every surface keeps the LOGICAL extent it has - a window is the same size on the desk after the scale changes - and its PHYSICAL extent becomes that logical extent times this ratio. So a scale change is a new generation with a new image set, exactly like a resize, and is told apart from one by the configuration: the same logical extent with a different scale is a scale change and nothing else is.  BOUNDED, because it decides an allocation. A ratio outside 1/8 .. 8/1, a zero on either side, or one that would take any surface past the service's maximum dimension is refused whole - no surface is reconfigured and the output keeps the scale it had. |
